question.text: A black body at a temperature of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>227</mn><mo> </mo><mo>°</mo><mi>C</mi></math> radiates heat at the rate of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>5</mn><mo> </mo><mi>cal</mi></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi> </mi><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo> </mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>. At a temperature of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>727</mn><mo> </mo><mo>°</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></math> the rate of heat radiated per unit area in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>cal</mi><mi> </mi><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math> is

solution.text:
According to Stefan's law radiant energy emitted by a perfectly black body per unit area per sec (ie, emissive power of black body) is directly proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature ie E∝T4

⇒ E1E2= T14T24

5E2= (273+227)4(273+727)4 

E2=5×10005004 

= 5×16=80 cal cm-2s-1
